name: LMV331TP-TR
title: LMV331TP / LMV393TP: 1.8 V to 5.5 V single and dual comparators with rail-to-rail inputs, internal hysteresis and open-drain outputs
summary: CMOS voltage comparators running from a single 1.8 V to 5.5 V supply, or split supplies of ±0.9 V to ±2.75 V, drawing 40 µA typ per channel. The input common-mode range reaches past both rails, the input bias current is 6 pA typ, and about 6 mV of hysteresis is built in. Each output is open drain; high-to-low delay is 120 ns typ. LMV331TP and LMV331TPU are single comparators in SOT23-5 or SC70-5 that differ only in where the two inputs sit; LMV393TP is the dual in SOIC-8, MSOP-8, TSSOP-8 or DIP-8. LMV331TP-TR is the single in SOT23-5 on a reel.
key_figures: 1.8 V to 5.5 V (±0.9 V to ±2.75 V split)
40 µA typ, 70 µA max per comparator
120 ns typ high-to-low, 250 ns typ low-to-high, 100 mV overdrive

tables.title: Absolute maximum ratings
notes: Note 1: Operating beyond these ratings can damage the part for good; staying at any of them for a long time can shorten its life.
Note 2: Each input has ESD diodes to both supplies. Once an input is more than 500 mV outside the supplies, hold its current below 10 mA.

Note 3: With an output shorted, the junction may need a heat sink to stay under its limit, the need set by the supply and the count of shorted outputs. The thermal figures hold for short traces to the leads; more copper changes them.

circuits.title: Figure 4. Non-Inverting Configuration with Hysteresis
circuits.description: The signal Vi reaches the non-inverting input through R1, and R2 feeds the output back to the same node, so the trip point moves with the output state. A reference Vr sits on the inverting input. RPU pulls the open-drain output up to VPU. The output goes high once Vi climbs to Vtr and returns low once Vi falls to Vtf.

parts.note: output back to the non-inverting input

circuits.title: Figure 5. Inverting Configuration with Hysteresis
circuits.description: The signal Vi drives the inverting input directly. R1 from VDD and R2 to ground set the non-inverting input, and R3 from the output to that node shifts it with the output state. RPU pulls the open-drain output up to VPU. With the output low, R2 and R3 act in parallel against R1; with it high, R1 and R3 act in parallel against R2.

parts.note: output back to the non-inverting input

equations.name: Internal offset and hysteresis
equations.expr: Vhyst = Vtr - Vtf; Vos = (Vtr + Vtf) / 2 - Vin-

where.Vtr: trip point for a rising input
where.Vtf: trip point for a falling input
where.Vin-: voltage held on the fixed input

equations.name: Non-inverting: rising trip point
equations.expr: Vr = R2 / (R1 + R2) × Vtr; Vtr = (R1 + R2) / R2 × Vr

where.Vtr: input level at which the output goes high

equations.name: Non-inverting: falling trip point
equations.expr: Vr = (VDD - Vtf) × R1 / (R1 + R2 + RPU) + Vtf; Vtf = (R1 + R2 + RPU) / (R2 + RPU) × Vr - R1 / (R2 + RPU) × VDD

where.Vtf: input level at which the output goes low

equations.name: Inverting: falling trip point
equations.expr: Vtf = R2 || R3 / (R2 || R3 + R1) × VDD

equations.name: Inverting: hysteresis
equations.expr: Vhyst = Vtr - Vtf = R1 || R2 / (R1 || R2 + R3) × VDD

operation.text: The CMOS input stage keeps the output from inverting when an input is driven past either supply. With VDD = 5 V, a sine running from about -0.3 V to 5.3 V still gives a clean square output.

Each input passes through a 1 kΩ series resistor to the core, with diodes from the pin to both supplies that clamp inputs driven beyond the rails. Large differential inputs beyond the supply voltage can damage the input stage.

Built-in hysteresis gives separate rising and falling trip points, so noise or stray feedback near the crossing does not make the output oscillate. The offset is measured as the midpoint of the two trip points relative to the fixed input. Swapping the inputs gives the same picture with the output inverted.

More hysteresis can be added with resistors, reducing chatter on slowly moving inputs and keeping a system from toggling too often, as in thermostat control. Chatter also raises dynamic supply current.

Input bias current is in the pA range, so high-impedance sources work, but board surface leakage matters: at low humidity nearby traces typically see 10^12 Ω between them, so a 5 V difference drives 5 pA, against a typical input bias of 6 pA at 27 °C. Route both inputs inside a multilayer board and surround the sensitive input with a guard ring held at the same voltage. Non-inverting use: bring the signal to VIN+ by a wire clear of the board and tie the guard to VIN–. Inverting use: tie the guard to VIN+ (the reference, such as VDD/2 or ground) and bring the signal to VIN– by a wire clear of the board.

The output swings to within 10 mV of either rail, and inputs can go 300 mV past either rail, so ground-level signals can be sensed. Output current capability rises with supply voltage. In a sustained output short keep the junction below 150 °C. The output has ESD diodes to both supplies; do not force it more than 0.5 V outside them.
All inputs and the output have reverse-biased ESD diodes; none may be biased more than 300 mV outside the supply rails.

Place a 0.01 µF to 0.1 µF bypass capacitor within 2 mm of the supply pin; a bulk capacitor of 1 µF or more within 100 mm supplies large, slow currents; other analog circuits may use the same one. Short leads and parts close to the pins reduce stray capacitance and noise.

Use an unbroken ground plane and a 0.1 µF surface-mount ceramic decoupling capacitor close to the supply. Keep input and output traces short and apart, with topside ground between them. Solder the part to the board, not into a socket. For slow inputs, 1000 pF or less across the inputs can stop oscillation through the transition, at some cost in delay when the source impedance is low. Run the ground trace under the part to the bypass capacitor to shield the inputs from the output.
